sessionTitle: Building WinUI Apps with C# First Patterns and AI Assisted Workflows

announcements.name: WinUI drops its version number, signaling long-term commitment
announcements.shortDescription: WinUI 3 will now be referred to simply as "WinUI" to convey there is no intention of building yet another new framework or a massive breaking change.
announcements.longDescription: In response to community questions about whether Microsoft is serious about sticking with the framework, the team announced that WinUI 3 (now four years old) will be referred to simply as "WinUI," dropping the version number to signal there is no intention of building yet another new framework or making a massive breaking change. The team is pushing to stretch WinUI to be accessible for any use case and is integrating it into the shell at a faster rate, with many first-party Microsoft features being built on top of WinUI. They emphasized commitment to moving WinUI forward and hope to see broader third-party and enterprise adoption.

announcements.name: Performance and quality investments shipped to the public Git repo
announcements.shortDescription: Improved memory usage and a switch to a system compositor are available to try today, with WinApp SDK experimental preview branches incorporating the changes shortly.
announcements.longDescription: Chris Anderson described core investments in performance, fundamentals, and quality, including heavily improved memory usage and a switch to a system compositor that should yield better performance improvements. These changes have already hit the public Git repo and are available to play with today, with WinApp SDK versions incorporating them coming shortly through the experimental preview branches.

announcements.name: New DataGrid and Charting controls coming to core WinUI
announcements.shortDescription: These data-oriented controls are due relatively soon and will ship in the core WinUI bits.
announcements.longDescription: The team is adding a lot of new controls, including DataGrid and Charting, which are up and coming and should be out relatively shortly. These will ship in the core WinUI bits and will enable a lot more data-oriented scenarios.

announcements.name: Open-source Phase 4 underway
announcements.shortDescription: The team is moving to work primarily and almost exclusively in public repos, landing pull requests publicly so the community can see and contribute to the work; Phase 3 (running tests in public) is already complete.
announcements.longDescription: Chris Anderson outlined WinUI's open-source journey, noting Phase 3 (running tests in public, so anyone can grab the bits, compile WinUI, and run tests) is already complete. The big next phase, Phase 4, moves the team from internal source repos to working primarily and almost exclusively in public repos, landing all pull requests on the public side. This is aimed at reaching a place where Microsoft can accept changes from the community, engage with it, and let the community see the work instantly.

announcements.name: C# elevated to a first-class way to target WinUI
announcements.shortDescription: The goal is to lift C# from XAML code-behind to a means of writing entire applications with full access to controls and templates currently locked behind XAML.
announcements.longDescription: Citing trends toward AI-assisted, code-first development with tools like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, and dynamic UI frameworks like SwiftUI, Compose, and React, the team wants to make C# a primary way to target WinUI. The goal is to elevate C# from being a way to do code-behind for XAML to a way to write an entire application, with full access to the existing WinUI framework's controls and templates. Several of those features are currently locked behind needing XAML, and the team wants to bring C# up to parity.

announcements.name: Microsoft UI Reactor experimental framework released
announcements.shortDescription: A new open-source, high-churn project for experimenting with new programming styles, controls, and app models, with proven ideas later pushed down into production WinUI.
announcements.longDescription: Microsoft UI Reactor is a newly announced experimental framework for experimenting with new styles of programming, new controls, and new app models. It is an open-source project, very early and with a high churn rate (code changing daily), intended as a place for community feedback, guidance, and participation, with PRs already landing from the community. As good ideas are found and baked, they will be pushed down into the production WinUI bits to become consistent and standard across the WinUI stack.
